front: What does a Commercial General Liability (CGL) policy insure against?
back: A CGL policy protects a business against claims of bodily injury, property damage, and personal and advertising injury arising out of its operations, products, or premises. It responds on behalf of the insured to third party claims, not to the insured's own property or first party losses.

front: What are the three insuring agreements of a standard CGL policy?
back: Coverage A (Bodily Injury and Property Damage Liability), Coverage B (Personal and Advertising Injury Liability), and Coverage C (Medical Payments). Each coverage part has its own trigger conditions and exclusions within the same policy form.

front: What does Coverage A of the CGL policy insure?
back: Coverage A insures the business against liability for bodily injury and property damage caused by an occurrence during the policy period. It is the broadest and most commonly claimed part of a CGL policy.

front: What does Coverage B of the CGL policy insure?
back: Coverage B insures against personal and advertising injury offences such as libel, slander, false arrest, wrongful eviction, and copyright infringement in advertising. It does not require bodily injury or property damage to trigger a claim.

front: What does Coverage C, Medical Payments, provide under a CGL policy?
back: Coverage C pays medical expenses for bodily injury to third parties on the insured's premises or from the insured's operations, regardless of fault, up to a small per person limit. It is a goodwill coverage meant to avoid larger liability claims.

front: How does an occurrence based CGL policy trigger coverage?
back: An occurrence based policy responds if the bodily injury or property damage happens during the policy period, regardless of when the claim is actually reported. Coverage can be triggered years after the policy expired as long as the injury occurred while the policy was active.

front: How does a claims-made CGL policy trigger coverage?
back: A claims-made policy responds only if the claim is first made against the insured and reported to the insurer during the policy period or an applicable extended reporting period. Timing of the claim, not the injury, is what matters most.

front: Why do claims-made forms typically include a retroactive date?
back: The retroactive date excludes coverage for injury or damage that occurred before that date, even if the claim is made during the policy period. It prevents the insurer from picking up losses from occurrences that took place before the policy relationship began.

front: What is an extended reporting period (ERP) in a claims-made policy?
back: An ERP, sometimes called tail coverage, allows the insured to report claims after the policy has ended for occurrences that took place before expiry. Without it, a lapsed claims-made policy leaves the insured with no coverage for late-reported claims.

front: What is the general aggregate limit in a CGL policy?
back: The general aggregate limit is the maximum the insurer will pay for all claims combined during the policy period, other than products-completed operations claims. Once this limit is exhausted, no further coverage is available regardless of remaining occurrences.

front: What is the products-completed operations aggregate limit?
back: It is a separate aggregate limit that applies specifically to bodily injury and property damage arising from the insured's products or completed work away from the premises. Having it separate from the general aggregate protects the general limit from being eroded by product claims.

front: What is the each occurrence limit under a CGL policy?
back: The each occurrence limit is the most the insurer will pay for bodily injury and property damage arising from a single occurrence. It is a sub-limit within the general aggregate and cannot exceed the aggregate for that policy period.

front: What is the personal and advertising injury limit?
back: It is the maximum amount payable for any one person or organization for offences covered under Coverage B, such as libel or wrongful eviction. This limit is typically part of the general aggregate rather than a separate additional amount.

front: What is the tenants' legal liability limit used for?
back: It applies to damage a tenant causes to a rented premises, most commonly fire damage, and is often shown as a separate sub-limit within the CGL policy. It fills the gap since a tenant has an insurable interest in premises they do not own.

front: Define the products-completed operations hazard.
back: It refers to bodily injury or property damage arising out of the insured's product or completed work, occurring away from premises the insured owns or controls, after the product has left the insured's possession or the work has been finished. It is what the products-completed operations aggregate limit is designed to cover.

front: When is work considered completed for products-completed operations purposes?
back: Work is considered completed when all work called for in the contract has been finished, when the work at a single job site has been finished, or when the portion of work done at a job site has been put to its intended use, whichever occurs first.

front: Why does products-completed operations coverage matter to a contractor?
back: A contractor remains liable for defective workmanship discovered after the job is finished and the crew has left the site. Without this hazard being covered, a claim arising after completion would fall outside the policy entirely.

front: What is the standard CGL exclusion for pollution?
back: The pollution exclusion removes coverage for bodily injury or property damage arising from the actual, alleged, or threatened discharge, dispersal, release, or escape of pollutants. The absolute pollution exclusion found in most current CGL forms applies whether the release was sudden and accidental or gradual; a sudden-and-accidental carve-back was a feature of older CGL wordings decades ago, not of current forms.

front: What is the professional liability exclusion in a CGL policy?
back: It excludes claims arising from the rendering of or failure to render professional services, such as advice, design, or specialized skill. Professionals need a separate errors and omissions policy to cover this exposure.

front: What is the intentional acts exclusion under a CGL policy?
back: It excludes bodily injury or property damage that is expected or intended from the standpoint of the insured. It preserves the insurance principle that coverage is for fortuitous, accidental events, not deliberate wrongdoing.

front: What is the care, custody, and control exclusion?
back: It excludes property damage to property the insured owns, rents, occupies, or has in its care, custody, or control. The rationale is that the insured should insure its own property under a property policy, not through liability insurance.

front: How does the workers' compensation exclusion in a CGL policy work?
back: It excludes any obligation the insured may have under a workers' compensation, disability benefits, or similar law, since those exposures are handled through the applicable workers' compensation board. Employer's liability coverage may be added separately for gaps not covered by the board.

front: What is the employer's liability exclusion and how is it typically addressed?
back: The employer's liability exclusion removes coverage for bodily injury to an employee arising out of employment, since it is normally handled by workers' compensation. Employers can buy back limited coverage for gaps such as claims not covered by the board through an endorsement.

front: What is the contractual liability exclusion and its exception?
back: The exclusion removes coverage for liability the insured assumes under a contract, except liability the insured would have anyway at law or liability assumed under an insured contract, which is specifically defined and brought back into coverage.

front: What is meant by an insured contract under a CGL policy?
back: An insured contract is a specific type of agreement, such as a lease of premises or certain sidetrack agreements, where the assumption of another party's liability is brought back into coverage despite the general contractual liability exclusion.

front: What does the aircraft, auto, and watercraft exclusion generally remove?
back: It excludes bodily injury or property damage arising from the ownership, maintenance, use, or entrustment of aircraft, autos, and certain watercraft owned or operated by or rented to the insured. Those exposures are addressed by separate auto, aviation, or marine policies.

front: What is the recall exclusion in a CGL policy?
back: It excludes the cost of withdrawing, recalling, inspecting, repairing, or replacing the insured's product or work if it is withdrawn from the market because of a known or suspected defect. Product recall coverage must be purchased separately.

front: What does the your product and your work exclusion under property damage generally address?
back: It excludes property damage to the insured's own product or the insured's own completed work itself, since correcting defective work or replacing a defective product is a business risk, not an insurable liability loss.

front: What is an additional insured endorsement used for on a CGL policy?
back: It extends coverage under the named insured's policy to another party, such as a landlord or project owner, for liability arising out of the named insured's operations. It is commonly required in lease and construction contracts.

front: What is a broad form CGL endorsement?
back: A broad form endorsement adds several extensions to the standard CGL policy, such as broadened contractual liability, broadened personal injury, and non-owned automobile liability, packaged together in one endorsement rather than purchased separately.

front: What is non-owned automobile liability coverage under a broad form CGL endorsement?
back: It extends liability protection to the business for vehicles it does not own but that are used on its behalf, such as an employee's personal vehicle used for business errands. It supplements rather than replaces the employee's own auto policy.

front: What is contingent employer's liability coverage?
back: It provides protection to the employer for bodily injury claims by employees that fall outside the scope of the applicable workers' compensation legislation, filling a gap left by the standard employer's liability exclusion.

front: What does the CGL definition of an occurrence generally require?
back: An occurrence is defined as an accident, including continuous or repeated exposure to substantially the same general harmful conditions. It requires an element of fortuity rather than a deliberate or expected event.

front: What does the term named insured mean on a CGL policy declarations page?
back: The named insured is the specific person or entity identified on the declarations page as the policyholder. Additional entities such as subsidiaries or additional insureds are covered only if they meet the policy's definition of insured or are added by endorsement.

front: Why is it important for a broker to confirm whether a CGL policy is occurrence or claims-made?
back: The trigger type determines when a claim must be reported and whether coverage exists for a loss discovered after a policy has lapsed. Failing to secure the right trigger, or an extended reporting period on a claims-made policy, can leave a client with an uninsured gap.

front: What is the difference between the general aggregate limit and the each occurrence limit?
back: The each occurrence limit caps payment for a single event, while the general aggregate limit caps the total paid across all occurrences during the policy period. A business with several claims in one term can exhaust the aggregate even if no single claim reaches the each occurrence limit.

front: What is a per project aggregate endorsement and why would a contractor want one?
back: It resets the general aggregate limit separately for each distinct construction project rather than sharing one aggregate across all of the contractor's work. It prevents claims on one project from eroding the limits available for other ongoing projects.

front: What triggers Coverage B for personal and advertising injury, unlike Coverage A?
back: Coverage B is triggered by specified offences, such as libel, slander, or invasion of privacy, committed in the course of the insured's business, rather than by bodily injury or property damage from an occurrence. Intent to commit the act, but not intent to cause injury, is typically required.

front: How do CGL policy limits apply when multiple claimants arise from a single occurrence?
back: All claims from the same occurrence are subject to the each occurrence limit collectively, even if multiple people are injured. Claimants share that single limit rather than each receiving a separate full limit.

front: What is the difference between defence costs inside the limits and outside the limits?
back: When defence costs are inside the limits, legal expenses reduce the available liability limit as they are paid. When defence costs are outside the limits, the insurer pays defence separately in addition to the stated liability limit.

front: Why do many commercial leases require the tenant to carry CGL insurance naming the landlord as additional insured?
back: The landlord wants protection if it is drawn into a lawsuit arising from the tenant's business activities on the leased premises. Naming the landlord as additional insured extends the tenant's own coverage to respond to those claims directly.

front: What common practice mistake occurs when a broker assumes CGL covers a client's own property damage?
back: CGL is third party liability coverage and generally excludes damage to the insured's own property through the care, custody, and control exclusion. The client needs separate commercial property insurance for their own building and contents.

front: What is a hold harmless or indemnification agreement in a commercial contract?
back: It is a contractual clause where one party agrees to assume liability that would otherwise fall on another party. Under the CGL contractual liability provisions, this assumed liability is only covered if the agreement qualifies as an insured contract.

front: What does the term subrogation mean in the context of a CGL claim?
back: Subrogation is the insurer's right to recover the amount it paid on a claim from a third party who was actually responsible for the loss. It allows the insurer to step into the insured's shoes to pursue the at fault party.

front: What is a waiver of subrogation and why might a contract require one?
back: A waiver of subrogation is an agreement where the insurer gives up its right to recover from a specified party after paying a claim. Contracts often require this so that one party's insurer cannot later sue the other contracting party for reimbursement.

front: What is completed operations liability distinguished from ongoing operations liability?
back: Ongoing operations liability arises from work still in progress, while completed operations liability arises after the work is finished and the insured has left the job site. Both are covered under a standard CGL policy but respond to different phases of a project.

front: What does the term insured premises mean on a CGL policy?
back: It refers to the locations described in the policy that the named insured owns, rents, or occupies for business purposes. Liability arising at those locations is generally covered, subject to the policy's other terms and exclusions.

front: How does a CGL policy typically define the insured for a corporation?
back: For a corporation, the definition of insured typically includes the corporation itself, its executive officers, directors, and stockholders while acting within the scope of their duties as such. It does not automatically extend to unrelated ventures they may pursue.

front: Why is products liability exposure a significant concern for manufacturers under a CGL policy?
back: A manufacturer can be held liable for bodily injury or property damage caused by a defective product long after it has been sold and is out of the manufacturer's control. The products-completed operations aggregate exists specifically to address this long-tail exposure.

front: What is the difference between property damage and bodily injury as defined terms in a CGL policy?
back: Bodily injury refers to physical injury, sickness, disease, or death sustained by a person, while property damage refers to physical injury to or loss of use of tangible property. Both are separately defined terms that trigger Coverage A.

front: What is loss of use coverage under property damage in a CGL policy?
back: Loss of use coverage responds when tangible property has not been physically damaged but the claimant has lost the ability to use it because of the insured's negligence, such as a utility outage caused by the insured's operations. It falls under the property damage definition.

front: Why might a business need a Commercial Umbrella or Excess Liability policy on top of its CGL?
back: An umbrella or excess policy provides additional limits above the CGL's underlying limits once those are exhausted, and can also broaden coverage for some claims not fully covered underneath. It protects against catastrophic liability judgments that exceed standard CGL limits.

front: What is the difference between a follow form excess policy and a stand-alone excess policy?
back: A follow form excess policy mirrors the terms and conditions of the underlying CGL policy, simply adding limits. A stand-alone excess policy has its own independent wording, which can create coverage gaps or broader coverage compared to the underlying policy.

front: What is vicarious liability and how does it relate to a CGL policy?
back: Vicarious liability is legal responsibility one party bears for the acts of another, such as an employer being liable for an employee's actions within the scope of employment. A CGL policy typically responds to vicarious liability claims arising from the insured's operations.

front: What is the difference between primary and non-contributory additional insured wording?
back: Primary and non-contributory wording states that the named insured's policy will respond first and will not seek contribution from the additional insured's own policy. It is often required by landlords and project owners to ensure their own insurance is not called upon first.

front: Why do construction contracts often require completed operations coverage to extend for a period after the project ends?
back: Defects in workmanship may not surface until well after a project is finished, so an owner wants assurance the contractor's coverage will still respond to claims discovered later. This is typically addressed by maintaining products-completed operations coverage for several years past completion.

front: What does the CGL policy mean by advertising injury offences such as misappropriation of advertising ideas?
back: It refers to using another party's advertising concept or style of doing business without permission, which can trigger a Coverage B claim. It falls under personal and advertising injury rather than the bodily injury and property damage coverage.

front: What is the significance of the deductible on a CGL policy?
back: The deductible is the amount the insured must pay out of pocket before the insurer's payment obligation begins on a claim. CGL deductibles can apply to indemnity only or to both indemnity and defence costs depending on the policy wording.

front: What is the difference between a self-insured retention (SIR) and a deductible?
back: With an SIR, the insured is responsible for handling and paying claims up to the retention amount before the insurer becomes involved at all, whereas with a deductible the insurer typically handles the claim from the start and is later reimbursed by the insured.

front: Why is it important to review the definition of your work carefully in a CGL policy?
back: The definition of your work determines what falls under the completed operations exposure and affects how several exclusions, such as the your work exclusion, apply. A narrow or broad definition can significantly change how much coverage a contractor actually has.

front: What is a claims-made policy's basic reporting requirement compared to occurrence coverage?
back: A claims-made policy requires the claim to be reported to the insurer within the policy period or extended reporting period, while an occurrence policy simply requires the injury or damage to have happened during the policy period regardless of when it is reported.

front: What happens to prior acts coverage if an insured switches from one claims-made insurer to another without matching retroactive dates?
back: If the new insurer sets a retroactive date at the start of its own policy rather than matching the prior insurer's earlier date, claims arising from acts before the new retroactive date may fall into a coverage gap unless a nose coverage or prior acts endorsement is obtained.

front: What is nose coverage in the context of claims-made policies?
back: Nose coverage, also called prior acts coverage, extends the retroactive date of a new claims-made policy backward to match an earlier date, closing the gap that would otherwise exist for occurrences before the new policy's normal retroactive date.

front: Why is products-completed operations often the largest exposure for a manufacturer purchasing CGL insurance?
back: A manufactured product can travel far from the point of sale and cause injury or damage long after leaving the manufacturer's control, creating potential claims years into the future. The products-completed operations aggregate is designed specifically to manage that long-tail risk.

front: What is the purpose of the supplementary payments provision in a CGL policy?
back: Supplementary payments cover costs such as the insurer's defence expenses, premiums for bail bonds, and certain expenses incurred at the insurer's request, typically in addition to the liability limits rather than reducing them.

front: What is the significance of the phrase legally obligated to pay as damages in the CGL insuring agreement?
back: It confirms that CGL coverage responds only when the insured has a legal liability for the loss, meaning fault or responsibility under law must be established, not simply that a loss occurred.

front: How does the CGL policy typically treat liquor liability exposures?
back: Standard CGL policies exclude liability arising out of causing or contributing to the intoxication of a person, or from violation of any statute related to the sale of alcohol, when the insured is in the business of manufacturing, distributing, selling, serving, or furnishing alcoholic beverages.

front: What is host liquor liability and how does it differ from a licensed liquor exclusion?
back: Host liquor liability applies to a business that occasionally serves alcohol as part of a social event, such as an office party, rather than being in the business of selling alcohol. It is often left intact under a CGL policy even where the liquor liability exclusion applies to licensed sellers.

front: What is the war exclusion in a CGL policy meant to address?
back: The war exclusion removes coverage for bodily injury or property damage arising from war, invasion, rebellion, or similar hostilities, since these catastrophic and uninsurable risks are outside the normal scope of commercial liability underwriting.

front: What does the CGL nuclear energy liability exclusion accomplish?
back: It excludes bodily injury and property damage arising from nuclear reaction, radiation, or contamination, since this exposure is instead handled through specialized nuclear energy liability pools due to its catastrophic potential.

front: How does the CGL policy generally treat asbestos exposures?
back: Most CGL policies contain a total or absolute asbestos exclusion, removing coverage for bodily injury or property damage arising from asbestos, given the severe long-tail latency and scale of asbestos related claims historically faced by insurers.

front: What does the phrase arising out of mean in the context of a CGL exclusion?
back: It is a broad causal connector used throughout CGL wording that courts have generally interpreted to require some meaningful causal relationship, but not necessarily direct or proximate cause, between the excluded activity and the loss.

front: Why do brokers recommend cross liability or severability of interests wording on a CGL policy?
back: Severability of interests wording treats each insured separately as if a separate policy had been issued to each, allowing one insured party to bring a claim against another insured under the same policy, which is important when a policy covers multiple related entities.

front: What is a named perils versus all risks distinction relevant to, and does it apply to CGL?
back: That distinction generally applies to property insurance, describing whether coverage is limited to listed perils or covers all causes of loss except those excluded. CGL liability coverage instead responds based on legal liability for an occurrence or offence, not a peril list.

front: What is the difference between duty to defend and duty to indemnify under a CGL policy?
back: The duty to defend is the insurer's obligation to provide a legal defence against a covered claim, which is often broader than the duty to indemnify, which is the obligation to pay damages the insured is legally required to pay once liability is established.

front: Why might an insurer defend a claim under a reservation of rights?
back: A reservation of rights lets the insurer provide a defence while preserving its right to later deny coverage if it is determined the claim falls outside the policy, often used when coverage is uncertain due to a potentially applicable exclusion.

front: What must a broker confirm about a client's CGL policy when the client takes on a new construction project as general contractor?
back: The broker should confirm that ongoing and completed operations for the new project are properly covered, that any owner-required additional insured and per-project aggregate provisions are in place, and that the policy has not excluded the type of work being performed.

front: What is a manuscript endorsement in the context of CGL insurance?
back: A manuscript endorsement is custom wording drafted for a specific client's needs rather than a standard filed form, often used to satisfy unique contractual requirements that standard endorsements do not fully address.

front: How should a broker respond when a landlord requires the tenant's CGL policy limits to be higher than the tenant currently carries?
back: The broker should discuss increasing the limits to satisfy the lease requirement, since failing to meet a contractual insurance requirement can leave the tenant in breach of the lease and without adequate protection if a large claim occurs.

front: What is the difference between an insured's operations and an insured's products for CGL purposes?
back: Operations refers to the ongoing activities and services the business performs, while products refers to tangible goods the business manufactures, sells, or distributes. Both create distinct liability exposures that a CGL policy is designed to address.

front: What role does the declarations page play in a CGL policy?
back: The declarations page identifies the named insured, policy period, limits of insurance, and the forms and endorsements that apply, serving as the summary reference point for the specific terms of that particular policy.

front: Why is it critical for a broker to review endorsements attached to a CGL policy, not just the base form?
back: Endorsements can add, remove, or modify coverage found in the base policy form, so relying only on the base wording without checking attached endorsements can lead to a broker missing important exclusions or restrictions that actually apply to the client.

front: What is the difference between the each occurrence limit and the personal and advertising injury limit within a CGL policy?
back: The each occurrence limit applies to Coverage A claims for a single event of bodily injury or property damage, while the personal and advertising injury limit is a separate cap specifically for Coverage B claims per person or organization.

front: How can multiple related businesses sharing one location create a CGL coverage gap if not properly structured?
back: If only one of several related businesses is named on the CGL policy, the other related entities may not qualify as insureds for claims arising from their own activities, leaving them exposed unless they are properly added as named or additional insureds.

front: What is the significance of the phrase during the policy period in the CGL insuring agreement?
back: It ties coverage to the specific dates shown on the declarations page, meaning the triggering event, whether an occurrence or a claim depending on the policy form, must fall within those effective dates for coverage to apply.

front: Why do many commercial contracts specify a minimum CGL each occurrence limit and aggregate limit?
back: Contracting parties want assurance that adequate funds will be available to satisfy a judgment or settlement arising from the contracted work, so they set minimum limits as a condition of doing business together.

front: What is the difference between bodily injury liability arising from products versus from premises operations?
back: Products liability arises from a defect in a good the insured manufactured or sold after it has left the insured's control, while premises operations liability arises from hazards present at a location the insured owns, rents, or occupies during current business activity.

front: What does it mean when a CGL policy is written on a Broad Form CGL basis in Canada?
back: A Broad Form CGL is a package of extensions added to the standard IBC CGL form providing broader contractual liability, broadened personal injury, tenant's legal liability, and non-owned automobile coverage together as a single enhanced product.

front: How does the CGL definition of insured contract treat an easement or license agreement?
back: Certain easement or license agreements can qualify as an insured contract depending on the specific wording used, but a broker must review the exact policy definition since not every contract automatically qualifies for the contractual liability exception.

front: What common misunderstanding do clients have about CGL and cyber liability exposures?
back: Clients often assume a CGL policy covers data breaches or cyber related losses, but most CGL forms now exclude electronic data and cyber exposures, requiring a separate stand-alone cyber liability policy to address that risk.

front: What is a key reason a broker should confirm the definition of pollutant carefully in a CGL policy?
back: The definition of pollutant can be extremely broad, covering substances like smoke, vapour, fumes, and waste, so a client operating in an industry with any incidental emissions may need a pollution liability endorsement to fill the gap left by the pollution exclusion.

front: Why does a CGL policy generally exclude damage to property being worked on by the insured?
back: Damage to that particular part of property on which the insured is performing operations is treated as a business risk of faulty work rather than an insurable third party liability exposure, consistent with the broader care, custody, and control rationale.

front: What does the term impaired property mean under a CGL policy and how is it treated?
back: Impaired property is tangible property, other than the insured's own product or work, that cannot be used because it incorporates a defective product or work of the insured but has not itself been physically injured. Loss of use of impaired property is typically excluded.

front: What is the sistership exclusion sometimes found in CGL policies?
back: The sistership exclusion removes coverage for the withdrawal, recall, or loss of use of the insured's products or work if a known or suspected defect is discovered in one unit, out of caution that other similar units may share the same flaw.

front: What is the difference between an occurrence policy's reporting clause and its trigger, and why does that distinction matter?
back: The trigger determines whether coverage exists based on when the injury happened, while the reporting clause sets out the insured's duty to notify the insurer promptly once aware of a claim or circumstance, even though late reporting on an occurrence policy does not usually eliminate the underlying trigger.

front: Why is it important for a broker to explain the difference between primary and excess CGL layers to a client with multiple policies?
back: Understanding which layer responds first ensures the client knows the order in which insurers pay, prevents confusion during a claim, and helps confirm that combined limits across layers actually meet contractual or risk management requirements.

front: What is the general purpose of the other insurance clause in a CGL policy?
back: The other insurance clause sets out how the policy responds when more than one policy could apply to the same loss, typically establishing whether the policy pays on a primary, excess, or pro rata basis relative to other applicable coverage.

front: Why should a broker review a client's CGL policy annually rather than only at inception?
back: A client's operations, revenue, contracts, and risk exposures can change significantly over a year, and coverage or limits appropriate at inception may no longer match the client's current exposures, creating gaps if not reviewed and adjusted regularly.

front: What is the practical difference to a client between a claims-made and an occurrence CGL policy when they eventually stop purchasing insurance or retire?
back: Under an occurrence policy the client remains protected for injuries that happened during any past active policy period, even after they stop buying coverage, while under a claims-made policy they generally need to purchase an extended reporting period to protect against claims made after coverage ends.

front: Summarize why understanding CGL policy structure, Coverage A/B/C, limits, exclusions, and the products-completed operations hazard together matters for a CAIB broker.
back: Together these elements determine exactly what third party liability protection a commercial client actually has, where the real gaps and sub-limits lie, and what endorsements or separate policies are needed, allowing the broker to properly advise clients and avoid uninsured exposures.

front: What is risk management, in the context of a commercial insurance client?
back: Risk management is the organized process of identifying, analyzing, and treating pure loss exposures facing a business, with insurance being only one of several available treatment tools.

front: What are the five steps of the risk management process, in order?
back: Identify the exposures, analyze and evaluate them (frequency and severity), select the appropriate risk management technique, implement the chosen technique, and monitor and review the results over time.

front: Why is exposure identification called the foundation step of risk management?
back: A loss exposure that is never identified cannot be analyzed or treated, so every later decision in the process depends on how thorough this first step is.

front: Name the four broad categories of loss exposure a broker should survey for a commercial client.
back: Property exposures, liability exposures, personnel (human resources) exposures, and net income (business interruption) exposures.

front: What is a physical hazard?
back: A physical hazard is a tangible condition of the property or operation, such as poor wiring or cluttered storage, that increases the chance or severity of a loss.

front: What is a moral hazard?
back: A moral hazard is a dishonest attitude on the part of the insured that increases the chance of loss, such as intentionally causing or exaggerating a claim.

front: What is a morale hazard?
back: A morale hazard is carelessness or indifference to loss arising from the mere existence of insurance, such as leaving a vehicle unlocked because it is insured.

front: What is frequency in loss exposure analysis?
back: Frequency is how often a particular type of loss is expected to occur over a given period, used together with severity to rank and prioritize exposures.

front: What is severity in loss exposure analysis?
back: Severity is the expected size, or dollar magnitude, of a loss if it occurs, and is analyzed alongside frequency to decide how a given exposure should be treated.

front: What are the four classic risk treatment techniques a broker can recommend?
back: Avoidance, reduction (loss control), retention, and transfer, often used together rather than as a single choice for any one exposure.

front: What is risk avoidance?
back: Risk avoidance means eliminating an exposure entirely by not undertaking or by discontinuing the activity that creates it, such as refusing to offer a hazardous product line.

front: What is a key limitation of risk avoidance as a technique?
back: Avoidance often means giving up a profitable activity along with its risk, and it cannot eliminate exposures that already exist from past operations.

front: What is risk reduction (loss control)?
back: Risk reduction is action taken to lower either the frequency or the severity of losses without eliminating the underlying activity, such as installing sprinklers or safety training.

front: Distinguish loss prevention from loss reduction within risk control.
back: Loss prevention aims to reduce the frequency of losses before they happen, while loss reduction aims to minimize the severity of a loss once it has already occurred.

front: Give an example of a loss prevention measure for a commercial client.
back: Installing security lighting and alarm systems to reduce the likelihood of a break-in is a loss prevention measure aimed at frequency.

front: Give an example of a loss reduction measure for a commercial client.
back: Installing a sprinkler system that limits fire damage after ignition is a loss reduction measure aimed at severity rather than preventing the fire itself.

front: What is risk retention?
back: Risk retention means the insured keeps the financial responsibility for a loss, either deliberately (planned retention) or unknowingly (unplanned retention).

front: What is planned (active) retention?
back: Planned retention is a deliberate decision to absorb a loss exposure internally, such as choosing a higher deductible after evaluating that the exposure is affordable.

front: What is unplanned (passive) retention?
back: Unplanned retention occurs when an exposure is retained because it was never identified or was mistakenly believed to be insured, leaving the business exposed by accident.

front: Why is unplanned retention the most dangerous form of retention?
back: Because the business has no funding plan for the loss and may discover the gap only after a claim is denied, causing a financial shock the client never budgeted for.

front: What is risk transfer?
back: Risk transfer shifts the financial burden of a potential loss to another party, most commonly an insurer through an insurance policy, but also through contracts such as leases.

front: Name a non-insurance method of risk transfer a broker might see in a commercial lease.
back: A hold harmless or indemnification clause in a lease or service contract, which shifts responsibility for certain losses to the other contracting party.

front: What factor most often determines whether an exposure should be retained versus transferred?
back: The severity of a potential loss relative to the client's financial capacity; low-severity exposures are commonly retained while high-severity exposures are usually transferred.

front: How does a deductible reflect a combination of retention and transfer?
back: The insured retains losses up to the deductible amount while the insurer accepts (transfer) responsibility for losses above that amount under the policy.

front: What is a captive insurance company, in a risk financing context?
back: A captive is an insurance company formed and owned by a business (or group of businesses) to fund and manage its own risk, a formal method of planned retention.

front: What is self-insurance?
back: Self-insurance is a formal, funded program of planned retention in which a business sets aside its own reserves to pay for losses rather than transferring the risk to an insurer.

front: What role does the broker play as risk management advisor?
back: The broker helps the client identify exposures, recommends appropriate combinations of avoidance, reduction, retention, and transfer, and places the insurance that fits the resulting program.

front: Why should a broker conduct a physical inspection of a commercial risk rather than relying only on the application?
back: A physical inspection can reveal hazards, unsafe practices, or exposures the client did not think to disclose, giving the broker a fuller and more accurate picture of the risk.

front: What is a hazard survey (or risk survey)?
back: A hazard survey is a systematic on-site review of a client's premises and operations used to identify physical hazards and loss exposures before recommending coverage.

front: What is a checklist approach to exposure identification?
back: A checklist approach uses standardized lists of common property, liability, personnel, and net income exposures to systematically prompt the broker through a client's risk profile.

front: What is a flowchart approach to exposure identification?
back: A flowchart approach traces the client's operations step by step, from raw materials through production to delivery, to identify exposures at each stage of the business process.

front: What is a financial statement approach to exposure identification?
back: A financial statement approach reviews the client's balance sheet and income statement to uncover assets, liabilities, and revenue streams that represent potential loss exposures.

front: Why should a broker use more than one exposure identification method?
back: Each method has blind spots, so combining checklists, flowcharts, and financial statement review reduces the chance that a significant exposure is missed.

front: How does business size and complexity affect the risk management process?
back: Larger and more complex businesses generally face a wider range of exposures and may justify more formal, ongoing risk management programs, while smaller businesses may rely more heavily on the broker's periodic review.

front: What is contingent business interruption exposure?
back: Contingent business interruption exposure is the risk of lost income caused by damage to a key supplier's or customer's premises rather than the insured's own property.

front: What is the difference between direct loss and indirect (consequential) loss?
back: A direct loss is the immediate damage to property, such as fire damage to a building, while an indirect loss is the resulting consequence, such as lost income while the building is repaired.

front: Why must risk management be treated as an ongoing process rather than a one-time exercise?
back: A business's operations, assets, and exposures change over time, so exposures must be periodically reidentified and the treatment plan adjusted to remain effective.

front: What is the monitoring and review step of the risk management process meant to accomplish?
back: It confirms that the chosen treatment techniques are still working as intended and flags new or changed exposures so the program can be updated.

front: How can insurance itself function as a loss control incentive?
back: Insurers often offer premium credits or require risk improvement measures, such as sprinklers or security systems, which encourages clients to adopt loss control alongside transfer.

front: What is the cost-benefit consideration a broker should raise before recommending a loss control measure?
back: The cost of implementing the measure should be weighed against the expected reduction in loss frequency or severity, since some controls are not economically justified.

front: What is a peril, as distinguished from a hazard?
back: A peril is the actual cause of a loss, such as fire or theft, while a hazard is a condition that increases the likelihood or severity of that peril causing a loss.

front: How does a broker's advisory role differ from a pure sales role?
back: As an advisor the broker analyzes the client's exposures and recommends a full risk management strategy, while a pure sales role would simply place whatever coverage the client requests.

front: What duty does a broker generally owe a commercial client regarding coverage gaps discovered during exposure identification?
back: The broker should advise the client of any material exposure or coverage gap discovered, so the client can make an informed decision on how to treat it.

front: Why should retention decisions be documented in the client file?
back: Documenting a client's deliberate choice to retain a risk protects the broker by evidencing that the exposure was disclosed and the decision was the client's informed choice.

front: What is a risk management manual, and why might a larger commercial client maintain one?
back: A risk management manual is a written record of a business's identified exposures, treatment techniques, and procedures, used to maintain consistency and support renewals and audits.

front: How does segregation of exposures function as a loss control technique?
back: Segregation spreads assets or operations across separate locations so a single event cannot damage the entire exposure at once, reducing maximum probable loss.

front: What is duplication as a loss control technique?
back: Duplication means keeping backup copies of critical records, equipment, or supplies so a single loss does not halt operations entirely.

front: How should a broker approach an exposure with high severity but very low frequency?
back: Even a rare event can be catastrophic, so high-severity exposures are generally recommended for transfer through insurance rather than retention, regardless of low frequency.

front: How should a broker approach an exposure with high frequency but low severity?
back: Frequent, low-severity losses are often better handled through retention or loss control, since insuring every small loss can be more costly than the losses themselves.

front: What is the difference between a maximum possible loss and a maximum probable loss?
back: Maximum possible loss is the worst-case total loss under the most extreme circumstances, while maximum probable loss is a more realistic estimate of the worst loss likely to occur given normal conditions.

front: Why is employee training considered a personnel-related loss control measure?
back: Trained employees are less likely to cause accidents or liability incidents, reducing both the frequency and severity of losses tied to human error.

front: What is a hold harmless agreement's effect on risk transfer in a construction contract?
back: It shifts liability for certain losses from one contracting party to another, often the contractor to the subcontractor, and is usually backed by an insurance requirement in the contract.

front: Why do many commercial contracts require proof of insurance alongside a hold harmless clause?
back: Requiring proof of insurance ensures the party accepting the transferred liability actually has the financial capacity to honour the indemnification obligation.

front: What is an example of avoidance applied to a liability exposure rather than a property exposure?
back: A business declining to install playground equipment for customers' children, thereby avoiding the premises liability exposure that equipment would create.

front: How does inflation protection relate to risk retention on property values?
back: Underinsuring due to outdated valuations creates unplanned retention, since the client unknowingly bears the gap between the actual replacement cost and the lower insured amount.

front: What ongoing broker activity helps prevent unplanned retention over time?
back: Regular policy reviews and updated valuations at renewal help catch new or growing exposures before they become unplanned retention through underinsurance.

front: Why is net income exposure often overlooked compared to property and liability exposures?
back: Net income exposure is intangible and only becomes apparent after a direct loss interrupts operations, so it is easy to underestimate until business interruption coverage is actually needed.

front: What is a risk management committee, and why might a mid-sized commercial client form one?
back: A risk management committee is an internal group responsible for overseeing exposure identification and treatment decisions, helping ensure risk management stays a continuous priority rather than an annual afterthought.

front: How does the broker's advisory role support the retention-versus-transfer decision specifically?
back: The broker quantifies the client's risk tolerance and financial capacity, then recommends which exposures the client can safely retain and which should be transferred to an insurer.

front: Summarize why combining multiple risk treatment techniques is usually better than relying on one alone.
back: Most businesses face a mix of exposures with different frequency and severity profiles, so a blended program of avoidance, reduction, retention, and transfer addresses each exposure more efficiently than any single technique applied uniformly.

front: What are the two main sources of law in Canada that a broker must understand?
back: Common law, which governs every province and territory except Quebec, and the Quebec Civil Code, which governs private law in Quebec. Common law develops through judicial precedent, while the Civil Code is a comprehensive written statute.

front: What is stare decisis?
back: The legal doctrine that courts must follow precedents set by higher courts in previous, similar cases. It creates consistency and predictability in common law jurisdictions.

front: What is the highest court in Canada?
back: The Supreme Court of Canada. It is the final court of appeal for all matters, including provincial civil, criminal, and constitutional cases, and its decisions bind every court in the country.

front: Name the general hierarchy of courts in a typical Canadian province.
back: Provincial or territorial court, then superior court (trial division), then provincial court of appeal, then the Supreme Court of Canada. Superior courts have inherent jurisdiction over most civil claims.

front: What is a tort?
back: A civil wrong, other than a breach of contract, that causes a person to suffer loss or harm, resulting in legal liability for the person who commits the act. Tort law is the foundation of most liability insurance claims.

front: What is the key difference between a tort claim and a breach of contract claim?
back: A tort claim arises from a duty imposed by law regardless of any agreement between the parties, while a breach of contract claim arises from a duty the parties voluntarily created between themselves.

front: What are the three main categories of torts?
back: Intentional torts, negligence, and strict liability. Liability insurance policies are primarily concerned with negligence, though some intentional acts may also trigger coverage disputes.

front: What is negligence, in tort law terms?
back: The failure to exercise the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would exercise in similar circumstances, resulting in harm to another person. It is the most common basis for liability claims.

front: What four elements must a plaintiff prove to succeed in a negligence claim?
back: The defendant owed the plaintiff a duty of care, the defendant breached the standard of care, the breach caused the plaintiff's loss, and the plaintiff suffered actual, provable damages (loss or harm) as a result.

front: What is duty of care?
back: A legal obligation requiring a person to avoid acts or omissions that could reasonably be foreseen to cause harm to others. It is the threshold question in every negligence analysis.

front: What is the neighbour principle, and where did it originate?
back: The idea that a person must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions likely to injure their neighbour, meaning anyone closely and directly affected by their conduct. It originated in the 1932 UK case Donoghue v Stevenson.

front: What is the standard of care?
back: The degree of caution and prudence required of a person to avoid liability for negligence, typically measured against what a reasonable person would do in the same circumstances.

front: How does the standard of care change for a professional, such as an insurance broker?
back: A professional is held to the standard of a reasonably competent member of that profession, not an ordinary person, because clients rely on the professional's specialized skill and knowledge.

front: What does causation mean in a negligence claim?
back: The plaintiff must show a direct link between the defendant's breach of duty and the harm suffered, often tested using the but for test, meaning the harm would not have occurred but for the defendant's conduct.

front: What is the but for test?
back: A test for factual causation asking whether the plaintiff's injury would have occurred but for the defendant's negligent act. If the injury would have happened anyway, causation is not established.

front: What is meant by remoteness of damage in negligence law?
back: The principle that a defendant is only liable for damages that were a reasonably foreseeable consequence of their negligent act, not for every consequence that technically flows from it, however unlikely.

front: What is contributory negligence?
back: A defence where the defendant argues the plaintiff's own carelessness contributed to their loss, which can reduce the damages awarded in proportion to the plaintiff's degree of fault.

front: How do most Canadian provinces apportion damages under contributory negligence?
back: Provincial negligence acts generally allow courts to apportion damages between the parties based on their relative degree of fault, rather than barring recovery entirely as older common law once did.

front: What is voluntary assumption of risk?
back: A defence, sometimes called volenti non fit injuria, where the defendant argues the plaintiff knowingly and willingly accepted the risk of harm involved in an activity, barring recovery.

front: What is vicarious liability?
back: A legal doctrine holding one party responsible for the wrongful acts of another because of the relationship between them, most commonly an employer being held liable for an employee's negligence committed within the scope of employment.

front: What is the key test for whether an employer is vicariously liable for an employee's act?
back: Whether the wrongful act occurred within the scope of employment, meaning it was authorized, or was an unauthorized way of doing something the employee was authorized to do, closely connected to their duties.

front: Is an employer generally vicariously liable for an independent contractor's negligence?
back: Generally no. Vicarious liability typically applies to employer-employee relationships, not to independent contractors, because the hiring party does not control the manner in which the contractor performs the work.

front: Why does vicarious liability matter to a commercial insurance broker?
back: It means a client's business can be held liable for the negligent acts of its own employees, so a Commercial General Liability policy must respond to claims arising from employee conduct performed within their job duties.

front: What is defamation?
back: A false statement communicated to a third party that harms another person's reputation. It includes both libel, which is written or recorded, and slander, which is spoken.

front: What is the difference between libel and slander?
back: Libel is defamation in a permanent form such as writing, print, or broadcast, while slander is defamation in a transient form such as spoken words. Libel is generally treated as more serious because of its lasting nature.

front: What are the elements a plaintiff must prove in a defamation claim?
back: The statement was made to a third party, it referred to the plaintiff, and it was defamatory in that it would tend to lower the plaintiff's reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person.

front: What is the defence of truth in a defamation action?
back: Also called justification, it is a complete defence because a defamatory statement is only actionable if it is false. If the defendant proves the statement is substantially true, the claim fails.

front: What is qualified privilege as a defence to defamation?
back: A defence protecting statements made honestly and without malice in situations where the speaker has a legal, moral, or social duty to communicate the information and the recipient has a corresponding interest in receiving it.

front: Why is personal injury and advertising injury liability important for a broker to understand?
back: Because Commercial General Liability policies typically provide coverage for offences such as libel, slander, and defamation under a personal injury or personal and advertising injury insuring agreement, separate from bodily injury coverage.

front: What is strict liability in tort law?
back: Liability imposed on a defendant regardless of fault or intent, typically applied to inherently dangerous activities. The plaintiff need only prove the activity caused harm, not that the defendant was careless.

front: What is the rule in Rylands v Fletcher?
back: A common law principle imposing strict liability on a person who brings something dangerous onto their land that is likely to cause harm if it escapes, even without proof of negligence.

front: What is occupiers' liability?
back: The legal duty owed by a person who occupies or controls premises to ensure the property is reasonably safe for people who enter it, forming the basis for most slip and fall claims against businesses.

front: What is the general standard imposed by occupiers' liability legislation in most Canadian provinces?
back: The occupier must take reasonable care to see that persons entering the premises, and their property, are reasonably safe while on the premises, regardless of whether the visitor is an invitee, licensee, or in some provinces a trespasser.

front: What is nuisance in tort law?
back: An unreasonable interference with a person's use and enjoyment of their land, such as excessive noise, odour, or vibration originating from a neighbouring property.

front: What is the difference between private nuisance and public nuisance?
back: Private nuisance affects a specific individual's use and enjoyment of their own land, while public nuisance affects the rights of the community or public at large, such as blocking a public roadway.

front: What is trespass to land?
back: The intentional and direct interference with another person's possession of land without lawful justification. Unlike negligence, trespass does not require proof of actual damage.

front: What is joint and several liability?
back: A rule allowing a plaintiff to recover the full amount of damages from any one of multiple defendants found liable, leaving that defendant to seek contribution from the others in proportion to their fault.

front: Why does joint and several liability matter to a broker placing commercial liability coverage?
back: A client with only minor fault could still be required to pay the entire judgment if co-defendants are unable to pay, making adequate liability limits important even when a client's own conduct was only partly responsible.

front: What is a limitation period?
back: A statutory time limit within which a legal action must be started, after which the claim is generally barred. Limitation periods vary by province and by the type of claim.

front: What is the general basic limitation period in most Canadian provinces for a civil claim?
back: Most provinces have adopted a general two year basic limitation period running from the date the claim was discovered, though specific exceptions and extensions apply depending on the province and claim type.

front: What is the discoverability rule?
back: The principle that a limitation period begins to run not necessarily from the date of the wrongful act, but from the date the plaintiff knew or ought reasonably to have known that they had a claim.

front: What is the burden of proof in a Canadian civil liability lawsuit?
back: The plaintiff must prove their case on a balance of probabilities, meaning it is more likely than not that the defendant is liable. This is a lower threshold than the criminal standard of beyond a reasonable doubt.

front: What are compensatory damages?
back: Monetary awards intended to restore the plaintiff, as far as money can, to the position they would have been in had the tort not occurred, covering both economic and non-economic losses.

front: What is the difference between general damages and special damages?
back: General damages compensate for losses that cannot be precisely calculated, such as pain and suffering, while special damages compensate for quantifiable out of pocket losses, such as medical bills or lost wages.

front: What are punitive damages?
back: Damages awarded not to compensate the plaintiff but to punish the defendant for particularly harsh, malicious, or reprehensible conduct and to deter similar conduct in the future. They are awarded rarely in Canada.

front: What is the Canadian cap on non-pecuniary damages for pain and suffering?
back: A trilogy of 1978 Supreme Court of Canada decisions established an upper limit on non-pecuniary damages for catastrophic personal injury, which is adjusted for inflation and now sits well above the original figure.

front: How is the Quebec Civil Code different from common law in structure?
back: The Civil Code is a comprehensive codified body of law that judges apply and interpret, while common law relies primarily on accumulated judicial precedent, though courts in both systems still consider prior decisions for guidance.

front: What is the Quebec Civil Code equivalent of a common law tort?
back: Extra-contractual civil liability, sometimes called delictual liability, which serves a similar function to tort law by imposing an obligation to compensate for harm caused by fault outside of a contract.

front: Why does a national insurance broker need at least a basic understanding of Quebec's civil law system?
back: Because policies and claims involving Quebec risks or Quebec residents are governed by the Civil Code rather than common law principles, which can affect how liability, damages, and contractual obligations are interpreted.

front: What is res ipsa loquitur?
back: A Latin phrase meaning the thing speaks for itself, an evidentiary principle allowing an inference of negligence when an accident is of a type that would not normally occur without negligence and the cause was within the defendant's control.

front: What is a fiduciary duty, and why does it matter to an insurance broker?
back: A fiduciary duty is a heightened legal obligation to act in another person's best interests with utmost good faith. Some Canadian courts have found brokers owe clients fiduciary-like obligations because of the trust and reliance involved in the relationship.

front: What is errors and omissions exposure for a broker rooted in?
back: It is rooted in the tort of negligence and the broker's professional duty of care to clients, arising when a broker fails to procure requested coverage, fails to advise of a gap, or otherwise falls below the standard of a reasonably competent broker.

front: What is the difference between an intentional tort and negligence?
back: An intentional tort requires the defendant to have intended the act that caused harm, such as assault or trespass, while negligence only requires a failure to meet a reasonable standard of care, with no intent to cause harm required.

front: What is contribution and indemnity between co-defendants?
back: The legal right of a defendant who has paid more than their proportionate share of damages to recover the excess from other defendants who share responsibility for the same loss, governed by provincial negligence legislation.

front: What is the role of the Federal Court of Canada?
back: It hears matters within federal jurisdiction, such as claims involving federal boards, maritime law, intellectual property, and disputes between the federal government and citizens, and does not generally hear typical provincial tort claims.

front: What is a class action, and why is it relevant to commercial liability insurance?
back: A class action allows one or more plaintiffs to sue on behalf of a larger group with similar claims against the same defendant. It can dramatically increase a defendant's total liability exposure, making adequate limits and defence cost provisions essential.

front: What is the difference between an occurrence trigger and a claims-made trigger in a liability policy, in relation to when a tort happens?
back: An occurrence trigger responds based on when the injury or damage actually took place, while a claims-made trigger responds based on when the claim was first reported, regardless of when the underlying tortious act occurred.

front: Why do aggregate limits matter given how tort damages can accumulate?
back: An aggregate limit caps the total amount an insurer will pay for all claims within a policy period, which is important because a single negligent act, such as a defective product, can generate multiple claims and cumulative damages.

front: What is the proper party defendant concept, and why should a broker understand it?
back: It refers to identifying which legal entity is actually responsible for a wrongful act, which matters because a broker must ensure the correct named insured and any relevant additional insureds are properly identified on a liability policy.

front: Why is understanding tort law fundamental to a commercial insurance broker's job?
back: Because Commercial General Liability insurance exists to respond to a client's legal liability arising from tort claims, so a broker cannot properly assess exposures, recommend coverage, or explain a claim decision without understanding how negligence and liability actually work.

front: What is the basic distinction between ocean marine insurance and inland marine insurance?
back: Ocean marine insurance covers vessels, cargo, and liability arising from transport over the sea, while inland marine insurance, despite its name, has nothing to do with inland waterways. It instead covers goods in transit over land, mobile or unique-valuation property, and certain instrumentalities of transportation and communication such as bridges, tunnels, and communication equipment. Both trace back to the same marine insurance origins but split as trade moved onto land routes.

front: Why does inland marine insurance also cover some fixed property, not just goods in transit?
back: Inland marine grew out of transportation coverage but expanded through the nationwide marine definition to include instrumentalities of transportation and communication, such as bridges, tunnels, and pipelines. This historical expansion is why property that never moves can still be classed as inland marine.

front: What does a hull policy insure?
back: A hull policy insures the vessel itself, meaning its physical structure, machinery, and equipment. Modern Canadian hull forms are broadly all-risks in structure rather than named-perils, subject to standard exclusions such as war, strikes, wear and tear, and inherent vice. It protects the shipowner's financial interest in the vessel as an asset.

front: What is a cargo policy designed to protect?
back: A cargo policy protects the owner of goods being shipped against physical loss or damage to the cargo while it is in transit. It can be arranged as a single voyage policy or as an open cargo policy covering ongoing shipments.

front: What does marine liability insurance respond to?
back: Marine liability insurance responds to a shipowner's or operator's legal liability for injury, death, or property damage caused to third parties, such as collision damage to another vessel or cargo owned by others. It is distinct from hull and cargo coverage, which protect the insured's own property.

front: Define general average.
back: General average is a principle where, if a voluntary and reasonable sacrifice or expenditure is made to save a marine venture from a common peril, all parties who benefit share the loss proportionately. It applies even to cargo owners whose goods were not sacrificed, as long as the venture as a whole was saved.

front: Give a classic example of a general average act.
back: Jettisoning cargo overboard to lighten a ship in danger of sinking is a classic general average act. The owner of the sacrificed cargo can claim a proportionate contribution from the ship and all other cargo interests that were saved.

front: What three conditions must be met for a general average act to be valid?
back: The act must be voluntary and intentional, made in a time of real peril to the common venture, and reasonable in the circumstances. If any of these elements is missing, the loss is treated as a particular average instead.

front: Define particular average.
back: Particular average is a partial loss to a specific interest, such as the ship or one shipment of cargo, that is borne solely by the owner of that property or its insurer. Unlike general average, there is no sharing of the loss among all parties to the voyage.

front: How does particular average differ from general average in terms of who pays?
back: In particular average, only the owner of the damaged property, or that owner's own insurer, bears the loss. In general average, the loss is spread proportionately across all parties whose property was saved by the sacrifice, based on each party's contributory value.

front: What is a marine warranty?
back: A marine warranty is a promise by the insured that a particular fact is true or that a particular thing will or will not be done, and it must be exactly complied with regardless of whether it is material to the actual loss. Breach of a warranty can discharge the insurer from liability from the date of breach.

front: Name the implied warranty of seaworthiness in a voyage policy.
back: In a voyage policy, there is an implied warranty that the vessel is seaworthy at the commencement of the voyage, meaning fit in every respect to encounter the ordinary perils of the sea. This implied warranty generally does not apply in the same way to time policies.

front: What is the implied warranty of legality in marine insurance?
back: The implied warranty of legality requires that the adventure insured is lawful and, so far as the insured can control the matter, that it will be carried out in a lawful manner. A marine policy cannot indemnify an insured for losses arising from an illegal venture.

front: How does an express warranty differ from an implied warranty in marine insurance?
back: An express warranty is written directly into the policy, such as a promise that a vessel will not sail after a certain date or will maintain a certain classification. An implied warranty, like seaworthiness, arises automatically by operation of marine insurance law even though it is not stated in the wording.

front: What is the effect of breaching a marine warranty, even if the breach did not cause the loss?
back: Under traditional marine insurance principles, breach of a warranty automatically discharges the insurer from liability from the date of the breach, whether or not the breach had any connection to the actual loss claimed. This strict rule distinguishes marine warranties from ordinary policy conditions.

front: What is an open cargo policy and why do frequent shippers use one?
back: An open cargo policy automatically covers all shipments made by the insured within described terms, without needing a new policy issued for every voyage. Frequent shippers use it to avoid arranging separate coverage each time goods move, ensuring continuous automatic protection.

front: What is a certificate of insurance in ocean cargo shipping?
back: A certificate of insurance is a document issued under an open cargo policy that evidences coverage for a specific shipment, often required by banks or buyers under a letter of credit. It confirms to third parties that the goods in transit are insured without disclosing the full policy wording.

front: What does Institute Cargo Clauses (A) provide compared to (B) and (C)?
back: Institute Cargo Clauses (A) provides the broadest all risks style coverage subject to specific exclusions, while (B) and (C) provide progressively narrower coverage for named perils only. A broker should match the clause set to the client's risk tolerance and the value or fragility of the cargo.

front: What is a protection and indemnity club, often called a P&I club?
back: A P&I club is a mutual association of shipowners that provides liability coverage for risks not typically covered under a standard hull policy, such as cargo damage liability, crew injury, and pollution liability. Members share the risk on a mutual basis rather than buying coverage from a traditional insurer.

front: What is a collision liability clause, sometimes called the running down clause, in a hull policy?
back: The running down clause extends hull coverage to include the shipowner's legal liability for damage caused to another vessel and its cargo following a collision, usually up to a stated proportion of the insured value. It complements P&I coverage, which typically picks up the remainder and other liability exposures.

front: Why is marine insurance historically considered a specialized branch of insurance law?
back: Marine insurance developed its own body of case law and statutory rules, such as those reflected in marine insurance acts, long before general property and liability insurance principles were codified. Concepts like general average, particular average, and strict warranty compliance are distinctly marine in origin.

front: What does the term perils of the sea mean in marine insurance?
back: Perils of the sea refers to fortuitous accidents or casualties peculiar to transport on water, such as heavy weather, stranding, or collision, rather than ordinary wear and tear or the inevitable action of wind and waves. It is a named peril concept central to many marine policies.

front: How does inland marine insurance treat bailee's customers goods coverage?
back: Bailee's customers goods coverage under inland marine insurance protects a business, such as a dry cleaner or warehouse, against liability for damage to customers' property while it is in the bailee's care, custody, or control. It fills a gap left by standard commercial property or liability forms.

front: What is the nationwide marine definition and why does it matter to a Canadian broker?
back: The nationwide marine definition is the traditional framework describing what property and activities qualify for inland marine treatment, including goods in transit, instrumentalities of transportation, and certain classes of movable property. A broker uses it to determine whether a risk belongs in an inland marine form rather than standard property coverage.

front: What is a builder's risk marine policy used for?
back: A builder's risk marine policy, sometimes arranged under an inland marine form, covers a vessel or structure being built or repaired against loss during the construction period. It responds to damage that could delay or increase the cost of completing the project.

front: What is the significance of a bill of lading to a cargo insurance claim?
back: The bill of lading is a document issued by the carrier that serves as evidence of the contract of carriage, a receipt for the goods, and often a document of title. In a cargo claim, it helps establish the condition of the goods when shipped and the terms under which they were carried.

front: What is a marine survey and when might an insurer require one?
back: A marine survey is a professional inspection of a vessel's condition, often required before binding hull coverage on an older or higher value vessel, to confirm seaworthiness and identify any conditions needing repair. Insurers use survey findings to underwrite the risk and may impose warranties based on the results.

front: How is contributory value used in a general average calculation?
back: Contributory value is the value assigned to each interest in the venture, such as the ship, the freight, and each cargo owner's goods, that survived the peril and benefited from the sacrifice. Each party's share of the general average loss is calculated in proportion to its contributory value relative to the total.

front: What is a general average bond or average guarantee used for?
back: A general average bond or guarantee is a document signed by cargo owners, or their insurer on their behalf, agreeing to pay their proportionate share of a general average contribution before the cargo is released. It allows goods to be delivered promptly while the final adjustment is completed.

front: What does barratry mean as a marine peril?
back: Barratry is a wrongful act committed by the master or crew of a vessel to the detriment of the shipowner or cargo owner, such as intentional scuttling or theft, done without the owner's knowledge or consent. Many marine policies specifically name barratry as a covered peril.

front: A cargo owner ships goods under an open cargo policy and needs proof of coverage for a bank letter of credit. What document should the broker arrange?
back: The broker should arrange a certificate of insurance issued under the open cargo policy, confirming coverage for that specific shipment. This satisfies the bank's requirement without needing to issue an entirely new policy.

front: A ship's captain orders cargo thrown overboard to keep the vessel from capsizing in a storm, and the vessel and remaining cargo are saved. What marine principle applies?
back: This is a general average act, since the sacrifice was voluntary, made under real peril to the common venture, and reasonable in the circumstances. The owner of the jettisoned cargo can claim a proportionate contribution from all parties whose property was saved.

front: A single container of goods is damaged by rough handling during loading, with no threat to the vessel or other cargo. How is this loss classified?
back: This is a particular average loss, since it affects only that one interest and there was no common peril requiring a sacrifice for the benefit of the whole venture. The loss falls on the cargo owner or that owner's own cargo insurer alone.
